title: Moving away from fossil fuels: who pays?
summary: The General Assembly debates a timeline to leave coal, oil and gas, and who should pay for it: subsidies, a loss and damage fund, climate finance, border taxes, displaced people and the duties of States.

resolution.title: The transition away from fossil fuels and shared responsibility for its cost

preambular.text: Recalling the Charter of the United Nations and its purpose of achieving international cooperation in solving international problems of an economic, social or humanitarian character,

Reaffirming the Paris Agreement and its agreed goal of holding the rise in global average temperature to well below 2 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels and pursuing efforts to limit it to 1.5 degrees,
Recalling the finding of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change that it is unequivocal that human influence has warmed the atmosphere, the oceans and the land,

Recalling also General Assembly resolution 77/276 of 2023, adopted without a vote, which asked the International Court of Justice for an advisory opinion on the obligations of States in respect of climate change,
Taking note of the advisory opinion delivered by the International Court of Justice on 23 July 2025,

operative.text: Calls upon all States to publish national plans for a just and orderly transition away from fossil fuels, ending unabated coal power by 2040 and the use of oil and gas by 2050;
Decides that all States will end government subsidies for coal, oil and gas by 2030, while protecting poorer households that depend on cheap fuel;
Requests developed States to double their contributions to the Fund for responding to Loss and Damage within five years;

Urges developed States to raise climate finance for developing countries to at least 1.3 trillion United States dollars a year by 2035, well above the goal of 300 billion dollars a year agreed in 2024;
Encourages States to place a carbon charge on imports from countries with weaker climate rules, in line with trade law, so that emissions do not simply move abroad;
Requests the drafting of a framework that gives people displaced by climate change a legal status and safe ways to move, while helping them to stay in their homelands where possible;
Calls upon all States to comply with the obligations identified by the Court, including the duty to act with due diligence to prevent significant harm to the climate system;
Requests the Secretary-General to prepare a report, in consultation with Member States, on ways to help States meet those obligations.

author: Claude Sonnet (delegated), 4 Nov 2026; to be checked by B. Gough
